subject: strip width of line transects for orangutan nest survey

messages.author: 6def11695a514c8c
messages.subject: strip width of line transects for orangutan nest survey
parts:
Hello!

I am a complete beginner to distance sampling, but need to calculate orangutan nest density from nest counts along line transects.

The equation for nest density is Nest Density = N/(Lx2w), where N = number of nests along a transect, L = length of transect and w = the strip width. I think that strip width means the distance at which nests can be seen either side of the transect, accounting for the decrease in detectability with distance from the transect.

I'd like help to calculate w from my data set which I have attached, using distance sampling in r studio.

Any help would be greatly appreciated, thank you!
Toby

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] strip width of line transects for orangutan nest survey
parts:
Toby

Welcome to the list.  You have the general idea of the formula correct.  We commonly write the formula in this way:
where P_a is the probability of detecting a nest given it is within distance w of the transect.  The question is how to estimate this value P_a.  That estimate is derived from fitting a detection function to the perpendicular distances you have observed.

Your data are well organised, except the file lacks the actual length of each transect; you record the distance along the transect for each detection, but you do not include the total length of each transect.

With the addition of the total transect length for each transect, you should be able to read your file into R and load the Distance package.  Change the field name "Transect" to "Sample.Label" and the field name "Perpendicular.distance.(m)" to "distance". Within the package, there is a function ds() that fits detection functions to your data.  You then choose the most appropriate model for your data and produce estimates of nest density from the output produced by the summary  function.

All of these steps are described in an introductory example of analysing line transect data at this web address
https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-lines/lines-distill.html
Note that to convert your estimate of nest density to an estimate of orangutan density, you will need to provide additional information, namely a nest production rate and a nest decay rate.  Examples of including these multipliers is provided in another example we have online:
http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-mult/multipliers-distill.html
You can also watch lectures on fundamentals of distance sampling at this website
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/
If you have further questions, please send them along.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] strip width of line transects for orangutan nest survey
parts:
Hi Eric, that's really helpful thank you! With regard to the transect lengths, they are all varying lengths but exactly 1000m of each transect was surveyed for nests. Do I need to create an extra column in my spreadsheet labelled 'length' and have 1000m for all nests. Or do I need to add the survey location (e.g. the survey on E1 A = 100-1000m) to my data set, and if so, how do I do this correctly? 

With regards to calculating the orangutan density from the nest density, I have the parameters from a nearby study site. However, I would like to calculate my own value for nest decay rate, as it is highly variable and I have a long study of nest data (surveys every month for 18 months), from which I should be able to calculate the nest decay rate. However, I am unsure of how to do this. I have read that I need to use a Markov Chain analysis involving creating an identity matrix, but have no idea how to do this. Can you offer any solutions?

Finally, when calculating nest density, should I use the combined number of nests over all 18 months, or just from one month. 

Thanks, again!
Toby

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] strip width of line transects for orangutan nest survey
parts:
Toby

Comments upon the three questions you ask:
  • Create a field in your data frame called "Effort" and assign the value 1000 to all rows in the data frame for that field
  • Nest decay rate:  the example of indirect surveys I suggested to you in my previous email (http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-mult/multipliers-distill.html)   describes in detail (code included) how to produce an estimate of mean time to decay using logistic regression (code from Mike Meredith).  That example also provides citations to literature for you to examine.
  • 18 months: I don't know enough about your survey design to answer that question.  Did you walk your transects only once, or monthly,...
